patient.name: Graham Whitfield
patient.setting: Acute medical unit, then cardiac catheter lab and ICU
patient.complaint: Admitted with central chest pain; collapses on the ward

diagnosis.exam: Expect a collapse vignette (unresponsive, agonal gasps, no pulse) and questions on the rhythm (VF, pulseless VT, PEA, asystole) or the likely 4H/4T cause.

points: Graham, 64, admitted at 07:00 with crushing central chest pain.
Troponin pending; ECG showed anterior ST depression.
10:20: nurse finds him slumped in his chair.

steps.lead: Graham's likely **myocardial infarction** is the commonest trigger: ischaemia disrupts the heart's electrical activity.

points: Head tilt, chin lift: only **occasional gasps**.
No carotid pulse felt in 10 seconds.

steps.lead: Collapse, unresponsive, not breathing normally, no pulse: **recognise it and start CPR** now.

steps.q: Graham is unresponsive with occasional gasps. What do you do?
o: Call the arrest team and start chest compressions
Put him in the recovery position
steps.r: **Agonal gasps are not normal breathing.** Unresponsive + not breathing normally = cardiac arrest: call and compress.

steps.lead: Graham's heart has **stopped pumping**: no output, so no consciousness, no breathing, and death within minutes untreated.

visual.title: Graham's monitor
visual.caption: Chaotic, irregular waves with **no clear QRS complexes**: ventricular fibrillation. **Shockable**.

steps.lead: Graham is in **VF**, the commonest initial rhythm, and it is **shockable**.

visual.title: Contrast: asystole
visual.caption: No electrical activity. **Non-shockable**: CPR and adrenaline, find the cause.

steps.text: A gasping patient is not 'breathing'. **Agonal breaths** are a sign of arrest, not a reason to wait.

investigation.exam: Expect 'which test identifies the reversible cause': blood gas for potassium, bedside echo for tamponade, temperature for hypothermia.

steps.lead: While CPR continues, the team runs the **4Hs and 4Ts**. For Graham, **thrombosis** (coronary) is top of the list.

steps.title: 4Hs and 4Ts during CPR
nodes: Toxins / Thrombosis → antidote / thrombolysis or PCI
steps.caption: Each H and T has its own fix; finding one changes management.

steps.title: Venous blood gas during CPR
steps.text: Acidosis from no perfusion. Potassium and Hb normal, so no hyperkalaemia or bleed.

points: Trachea central; equal air entry with bag ventilation.
No drugs or overdose history; no leg swelling.

visual.title: Graham's end-tidal CO2 during CPR
visual.caption: A sudden rise in EtCO2 at 10 minutes signals **ROSC** before the pulse check.

steps.text: Exam pattern: the stem hides the cause. **Trauma + deviated trachea** = tension; **dialysis** = potassium; **post-op + swollen leg** = PE.

management.exam: Expect 'next most appropriate step': VF on monitor → **defibrillation**; adrenaline and amiodarone after the 3rd shock; adrenaline immediately in PEA/asystole.

steps.lead: The nurse pulls the **emergency buzzer** (999 outside hospital) and starts compressions at **30:2**.

visual.title: Compression rate
visual.label: Graham 110/min
visual.caption: Depth 5–6 cm, full recoil, minimal pauses.

steps.q: Pads on: the monitor shows VF. What next?
o: Continue CPR and give adrenaline first
steps.r: VF is shockable: **defibrillate** straight away. Synchronised shocks are for tachycardias **with a pulse**.

steps.lead: Graham gets the **ALS** algorithm: shock at **200 J**, CPR for **2 minutes**, check rhythm, repeat.

steps.title: Graham's shockable algorithm
nodes: Shock 3 → CPR; adrenaline 1 mg + amiodarone 300 mg
Adrenaline every 3–5 min if still arrested
steps.caption: Amiodarone 150 mg more if still VF after 5 shocks.

steps.q: After the 3rd shock, Graham is still in VF. Which drugs now?
o: Adrenaline 1 mg IV and amiodarone 300 mg IV
steps.r: After the **3rd shock** in a shockable rhythm: **adrenaline 1 mg** plus **amiodarone 300 mg**.

steps.lead: Graham's IV went in easily; had it failed, use **intraosseous** access. After **ROSC**: oxygen, treat the cause, ICU.

points: ROSC after the 4th shock; 12-lead now shows anterior ST elevation.
Straight to the cath lab: LAD occlusion stented.
Then ICU: ventilated, targeted temperature control.

steps.lead: Every step for Graham follows the **Resuscitation Council UK ALS** algorithm.

steps.text: **Adrenaline timing differs**: shockable = after the 3rd shock; non-shockable (PEA, asystole) = **immediately**. Amiodarone is never for PEA or asystole.
Special cases: pregnant over 20 weeks → **left lateral tilt ~15°**; PE → thrombolyse and continue CPR **60–90 min**.

science.exam: Expect applied mechanisms: how defibrillation works, why PEA is not shocked, adrenaline's alpha-1 action, amiodarone as class III.

steps.lead: Every minute without compressions, Graham's brain loses perfusion. **Early CPR** matters more than any drug.
His ischaemic myocardium went into **VF**. The shock depolarised a **critical mass** at once, letting the **SA node** take back control.

steps.title: How defibrillation works
nodes: Shock depolarises a critical mass of myocardium
SA node resumes as dominant pacemaker

steps.lead: If Graham had been in **PEA**, a shock would do nothing: the electrics work but the pump does not, usually from a 4H/4T.
Graham's **adrenaline** squeezed the periphery via **alpha-1**; **amiodarone** (class III) lengthened refractoriness to stop VF recurring.

steps.q: Why does adrenaline improve the chance of ROSC?
o: Alpha-1 vasoconstriction diverts flow to coronary and cerebral circulations
steps.r: **Alpha-1** peripheral vasoconstriction raises aortic diastolic pressure, so more blood reaches the heart and brain.

mcq.r: **VF and pulseless VT** respond to defibrillation.

mcq.q: Most common initial rhythm in sudden cardiac arrest?
Organised rhythm on the monitor but no pulse?
When is adrenaline given in a shockable arrest?
Route if IV access fails during arrest?
Receptor through which adrenaline improves ROSC?
mcq.r: **Alpha-1** vasoconstriction diverts flow to heart and brain.

technique.stem: A 70 year old man collapses in the coronary care unit two days after a myocardial infarction. He is unresponsive and has no palpable pulse. The cardiac monitor shows chaotic, irregular deflections of varying amplitude with no identifiable QRS complexes.
technique.q: Which is the most likely rhythm?

steps.x: A rhythm question in an arrest: decide shockable or not from the ECG description.
Post-MI, pulseless, chaotic trace with no QRS.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **VF**: the commonest initial arrest rhythm, shockable.

elim: Asystole is a flat line, not chaotic deflections.
AF has narrow QRS complexes and produces a pulse.
Pulseless VT shows regular broad QRS complexes.

steps.x: **E. Ventricular fibrillation.** Rule: no QRS + chaos = VF; regular broad = VT; organised = PEA; flat = asystole.

technique.stem: A 58 year old man on haemodialysis missed two sessions. He collapses at home and paramedics start CPR. In the Emergency Department the monitor shows a broad, slow complex rhythm without a pulse.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate investigation to identify a reversible cause?

steps.x: It asks for a test to find the reversible cause. Which H or T does the history point to?
Missed dialysis = hyperkalaemia; PEA.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A **blood gas** gives potassium in a minute.

elim: Too slow and not the likely cause.

steps.x: **E. Venous blood gas.** Rule: dialysis patient in arrest = check potassium on a gas.

technique.stem: A 78 year old woman has a cardiac arrest on the ward and chest compressions are started. The defibrillator pads are attached and the monitor shows ventricular fibrillation.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

steps.x: A next-step question in arrest: shockable or not decides it.
Arrest with a shockable rhythm.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Defibrillate**, then CPR for 2 minutes.

elim: VF needs a shock without delay.
Given after the 3rd shock in a shockable rhythm.
Airway can wait; the shock cannot.

steps.x: **B. Defibrillation.** Rule: shockable rhythm = shock first, drugs after the 3rd.

technique.stem: A 66 year old man in VF arrest is defibrillated. After the shock the monitor shows sinus rhythm and he has a pulse.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism by which defibrillation restored his rhythm?
o: Simultaneous depolarisation of a critical mass of myocardium

steps.x: A mechanism question: what does the shock physically do to the myocardium?
Shock ends VF and sinus returns.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The shock depolarises a **critical mass** at once; the **SA node** then takes over.
**D. Simultaneous depolarisation of a critical mass of myocardium.** Rule: defib resets the myocardium; it does not 'restart' it.

practice.stem: A 61 year old man is waiting in the clinic when he suddenly slumps in his chair. He does not respond to voice or pain. He is making occasional gasping noises. No carotid pulse is felt. Ten minutes earlier his pulse rate was 104 bpm and BP 146/90 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Collapse, unresponsiveness, agonal gasps and no pulse are the triad of cardiac arrest.

steps.x: The lead-in is "Which is the most likely diagnosis?" Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Unresponsive, agonal gasps, pulseless.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Cardiac arrest**.
**A. Cardiac arrest.** Recognise and start CPR.

practice.stem: A 55 year old man collapses on the cardiology ward. He is unresponsive and pulseless. A rhythm strip is recorded (see item resources).
practice.q: Which is the most likely rhythm?
practice.e: A regular broad-complex tachycardia (~150 bpm) without a pulse is pulseless VT, a shockable rhythm.

steps.x: The lead-in is "Which is the most likely rhythm?" Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Pulseless, broad regular complexes.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Pulseless VT**: shockable.
**D. Pulseless ventricular tachycardia.** Broad regular + no pulse = pVT.

practice.stem: A 72 year old woman collapses on the ward. CPR is started. The monitor shows narrow, regular complexes at 90 per minute, but no pulse is palpable.
practice.q: Which is the most likely rhythm?
practice.e: An organised rhythm without a pulse is PEA, which is non-shockable and usually has a reversible cause.

steps.x: The lead-in is "Which is the most likely rhythm?" Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Organised rhythm, no output.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **PEA**: non-shockable.
**B. Pulseless electrical activity.** Adrenaline immediately, find the cause.

practice.stem: A 24 year old man is brought in after a motorbike crash. He becomes breathless and then loses his pulse. Before arrest his pulse rate was 136 bpm, BP 74/40 mmHg. His trachea is deviated to the left and there are absent breath sounds on the right.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his cardiac arrest?
practice.e: Tracheal deviation away from a silent hemithorax in trauma is a tension pneumothorax, a reversible 4T cause.

steps.x: The lead-in is "Which is the most likely cause of his cardiac arrest?" Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: trachea is deviated to the left
absent breath sounds on the right
steps.x: Trauma, tracheal shift away, silent right chest.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Tension pneumothorax** (a 4T).

elim: Raised JVP and muffled heart sounds, trachea central.
Trachea central, no unilateral silent chest.
No trauma mechanism for tracheal shift.

steps.x: **E. Tension pneumothorax.** Decompress 2nd intercostal space.

practice.stem: A 79 year old woman is found unresponsive in her garden on a winter morning. She has no pulse and CPR is started.
practice.q: Which is the most likely reversible cause of her cardiac arrest?
practice.e: Exposure and a core temperature of 28°C point to hypothermia, one of the 4Hs.

steps.x: The lead-in is "Which is the most likely reversible cause of her cardiac arrest?" Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Exposure in cold and low core temperature.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Hypothermia** (a 4H).
**B. Hypothermia.** Warm while resuscitating.

practice.stem: A 67 year old man is 5 days after a total hip replacement. He becomes suddenly breathless and collapses. His left calf is swollen. Before collapse his pulse rate was 124 bpm, BP 88/56 mmHg and oxygen saturation 84% on air. He is now pulseless with PEA.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his cardiac arrest?
practice.e: Post-operative DVT with sudden hypoxia and PEA is a massive PE: a 'thrombosis' T.

steps.x: The lead-in is "Which is the most likely cause of his cardiac arrest?" Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Post-op, DVT, sudden hypoxia, PEA.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Massive PE**.

elim: Sudden breathlessness and calf swelling point elsewhere.

steps.x: **D. Thrombosis (pulmonary embolism).** Thrombolyse and continue CPR 60–90 min.

practice.stem: A 34 year old man has a stab wound to the left chest. He becomes pulseless in the Emergency Department; the monitor shows PEA. Before arrest his pulse rate was 128 bpm and BP 76/58 mmHg with distended neck veins and quiet heart sounds. His trachea is central.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate investigation to identify the cause?
practice.e: Penetrating trauma with raised JVP, quiet heart sounds and PEA suggests tamponade; bedside echo confirms it during CPR.

steps.x: The lead-in is "Which is the most appropriate immediate investigation to identify the cause?" Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: stab wound to the left chest
steps.x: Beck's triad after penetrating trauma.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Point-of-care echo** to see pericardial fluid.

elim: Slow and poor at showing tamponade.
Not possible during arrest and not diagnostic.

steps.x: **A. Bedside focused echocardiography.** Then pericardiocentesis or thoracotomy.

practice.stem: A 60 year old woman on haemodialysis missed her last two sessions. She collapses and CPR is started. The monitor shows a slow broad-complex rhythm with no pulse.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate investigation?
o: Urea and electrolytes sent to the lab
practice.e: Hyperkalaemia is a reversible 4H; a blood gas gives the potassium immediately during CPR.

steps.x: The lead-in is "Which is the most appropriate immediate investigation?" Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Missed dialysis + broad slow rhythm = hyperkalaemia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Blood gas** potassium.

elim: Too slow; a gas gives potassium in a minute.

steps.x: **B. Blood gas for potassium.** Then calcium, insulin-dextrose.

practice.stem: A 66 year old man collapses on the ward. He is unresponsive with no pulse. CPR is started. The defibrillator is attached and shows ventricular fibrillation.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Continue CPR (30:2) and reassess in 2 minutes
practice.e: VF is shockable: give an unsynchronised shock immediately; drugs come after the third shock.

steps.x: The lead-in is "Which is the next most appropriate step in management?" Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Arrest, shockable rhythm.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Defibrillation**.

elim: After the 3rd shock in shockable rhythms.

steps.x: **E. Unsynchronised shock (defibrillation).** Shock, then CPR 2 min.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man is in cardiac arrest. He has received three shocks for ventricular fibrillation and chest compressions have restarted. He remains in VF. IV access is in place.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate drug management now?
o: Adrenaline 1 mg IV and amiodarone 300 mg IV
practice.e: After the third shock in VF/pVT, give adrenaline 1 mg and amiodarone 300 mg once compressions restart.

steps.x: The lead-in is "Which is the most appropriate drug management now?" Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Shockable, after 3rd shock.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Adrenaline 1 mg + amiodarone 300 mg**.

elim: Amiodarone is also given after the 3rd shock.
150 mg is the further dose after 5 shocks.

steps.x: **B. Adrenaline 1 mg IV and amiodarone 300 mg IV.** Then adrenaline every 3–5 min.

practice.stem: A 75 year old woman is found in cardiac arrest on the ward. CPR is started. The monitor shows asystole. Before arrest her pulse rate was 48 bpm and BP 82/50 mmHg. IV access is in place.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate drug to give now?
practice.e: In non-shockable rhythms (PEA, asystole) adrenaline 1 mg is given as soon as access is obtained; no shock or amiodarone.

steps.x: The lead-in is "Which is the most appropriate drug to give now?" Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Non-shockable rhythm.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Adrenaline 1 mg immediately**, then every 3–5 min.

elim: That timing is for shockable rhythms.

steps.x: **A. Adrenaline 1 mg IV immediately.** No shock, no amiodarone.

practice.stem: A 62 year old man is in VF arrest. After the third shock he is given adrenaline 1 mg IV. His pulse rate before arrest was 110 bpm and BP 100/60 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism by which adrenaline improves the chance of ROSC?
practice.e: Adrenaline's alpha-1 vasoconstriction diverts flow to the coronary and cerebral circulations, improving the chance of ROSC.

steps.x: The lead-in is "Which is the most likely mechanism by which adrenaline improves the chance of ROSC?" Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Adrenaline during CPR.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Alpha-1** vasoconstriction redirects flow to coronary and cerebral circulations.
**A. Alpha-1 mediated peripheral vasoconstriction.** Raises perfusion pressure.

prompts.q: What is cardiac arrest and what are its common causes?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the stem gives you the trigger.

prompts.q: How do you recognise cardiac arrest at the bedside?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: agonal gasps are not breathing.

points.why: Do not mistake gasps for breathing.

prompts.q: Which arrest rhythms are shockable and which are not? Describe each.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the shock decision drives everything.
Exam thinking: each one has a clue in the stem.

prompts.q: How do you find the reversible cause during CPR?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: fast bedside tests only.

points.p: Blood gas: potassium, pH, Hb, glucose

points.why: Clinical clues for hypothermia and tension.

prompts.q: What is basic life support: who, ratio, rate and depth?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the numbers are tested.

points.p: Call for help (999) and start CPR

prompts.q: Describe the ALS algorithm for a shockable rhythm, including drug timing.

points.p: After 3rd shock: adrenaline 1 mg + amiodarone 300 mg
Adrenaline every 3–5 min; amiodarone 150 mg after 5 shocks

prompts.q: How do you manage a non-shockable rhythm and the special situations?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: adrenaline immediately, no shock.

points.p: PEA/asystole: CPR 30:2, adrenaline 1 mg immediately, no shock

prompts.q: How does defibrillation work, and why is PEA not shocked?

points.p: Shock depolarises a critical mass of myocardium; SA node resumes
PEA: organised electrics but no mechanical output; usually a 4H/4T

prompts.q: How do adrenaline and amiodarone work in arrest, and why does the brain suffer so fast?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: receptor, class, and perfusion.

points.p: Adrenaline: alpha-1 vasoconstriction, flow to heart and brain
Amiodarone: class III, prolongs action potential and refractory period
No output stops cerebral perfusion: hypoxic injury within minutes

glossary.Cardiac arrest: Sudden cessation of cardiac output, so circulation stops.
glossary.CPR: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation: chest compressions and rescue breaths.
glossary.BLS: Basic life support: recognition, calling for help, CPR and defibrillation.
glossary.ALS: Advanced life support: the hospital algorithm of shocks, drugs and reversible causes.
glossary.ROSC: Return of spontaneous circulation: a pulse returns.
glossary.Agonal gasps: Occasional, ineffective gasping breaths seen in cardiac arrest.
glossary.VF: Ventricular fibrillation: chaotic ventricular activity with no output; shockable.
glossary.Pulseless VT: Ventricular tachycardia without a pulse; shockable.
glossary.PEA: Pulseless electrical activity: organised rhythm on the monitor but no pulse.
glossary.Asystole: No electrical activity of the heart; a flat line.
glossary.Shockable: Rhythms that respond to defibrillation: VF and pulseless VT.
glossary.Defibrillation: An unsynchronised shock that depolarises the myocardium to stop VF or pVT.
glossary.Synchronised cardioversion: A shock timed to the R wave, used for tachycardias with a pulse.
glossary.4Hs and 4Ts: The reversible causes of arrest to look for during CPR.
glossary.Tension pneumothorax: Air trapped in the pleural space under pressure, shifting the mediastinum.
glossary.Tamponade: Fluid or blood in the pericardium compressing the heart.
glossary.Beck's triad: Hypotension, raised JVP and muffled heart sounds: signs of tamponade.
glossary.Hypovolaemia: Low circulating blood volume, for example from bleeding.
glossary.Hyperkalaemia: High blood potassium, which can cause broad complexes and arrest.
glossary.Intraosseous: Drug access through a needle into bone marrow.
glossary.Adrenaline: Catecholamine given 1 mg IV in arrest; alpha-1 vasoconstriction improves perfusion.
glossary.Amiodarone: Class III antiarrhythmic given 300 mg after the 3rd shock in VF/pVT.
glossary.Lidocaine: Antiarrhythmic used as an alternative to amiodarone in refractory VF.
glossary.Alpha-1 receptor: Adrenergic receptor on vessels that causes vasoconstriction.
glossary.Class III antiarrhythmic: Drug that blocks potassium channels, prolonging action potential and refractory period.
glossary.Refractory period: Time after depolarisation when a cell cannot fire again.
glossary.Critical mass: Enough myocardium depolarised together to stop chaotic activity.
glossary.SA node: The heart's natural pacemaker in the right atrium.
glossary.Aortocaval compression: The pregnant uterus pressing on the aorta and vena cava, reducing venous return.
glossary.Left lateral tilt: Tilting a pregnant patient about 15° to the left to relieve aortocaval compression.
glossary.Thrombolysis: Drug breakdown of a clot, such as alteplase for massive PE.
glossary.Alteplase: A thrombolytic drug used for massive PE and stroke.
glossary.Needle decompression: Wide-bore cannula into the 2nd intercostal space to release a tension pneumothorax.
glossary.EtCO2: End-tidal carbon dioxide; a sudden rise during CPR suggests ROSC.
glossary.Hypoxic brain injury: Brain damage from lack of oxygen, starting within minutes of arrest.
glossary.Post-ROSC care: Oxygen, treating the cause and ICU support after circulation returns.
glossary.PCI: Percutaneous coronary intervention: opening a blocked coronary artery with a stent.
